summary: The payments outage is caused by disk exhaustion on the shared ledger-db datastore, not by payment-service v6.0.0. An inactive replication slot ('analytics_cdc') retained tens of GB of WAL from ~13:02Z, driving disk_used_pct on a smooth ~1%/6-min ramp from 86.57% at 12:30Z to 100% at the 15:00Z bucket, where it stayed pinned through 16:54Z (F3, F21, F22, F23). Postgres then rejected all writes with hard 'No space left on device' errors (F2, F4), breaking three of the four shared-ledger-db writers — payment-service, order-service and settlement-service — at the same 15:00Z onset, while the v6.0.0 release is coincidental (it shipped at 14:46Z, ~1.5-2h after saturation began, and its 15:12Z rollback produced no recovery: error_rate held ~60% through 16:55Z on complete metrics). Confidence in H2 is 0.78 (high). The correct fix is to free disk on ledger-db (drop/repair the retaining replication slot and purge retained WAL), not to roll back the release.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared ledger-db disk exhaustion from retained WAL (inactive analytics_cdc replication slot) — hard write failures across co-tenant writers
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A replication slot on the shared ledger-db ('analytics_cdc', inactive but retaining tens of GB of WAL repeatedly from ~13:02Z) drove the datastore disk on a smooth monotonic ramp to 100%, where it stayed pinned for >2 hours. Postgres then rejected ALL writes (PANIC could not write pg_wal xlogtemp, could not extend base file), so every writer to the shared ledger-db — payment-service, order-service and settlement-service — got hard 'No space left on device' errors. The fault origin is the shared datastore (infrastructure), not payment-service code; the v6.0.0 release is coincidental.

causal_chain.claim: Inactive replication slot 'analytics_cdc' on shared ledger-db repeatedly retains tens of GB of WAL from ~13:02Z
WAL retention drives a smooth monotonic disk ramp: 86.57% (12:30Z) -> 89.37% (13:00Z) -> 90.40% (13:12Z) -> 97.48% (14:30Z) -> 99.88% (14:54Z) -> 100% at 15:00Z (no step change at the 14:46Z deploy)
ledger-db hits full disk and emits hard PANICs ('could not write to pg_wal/xlogtemp', 'could not extend file') at ~15:01Z
Disk stays pinned at 100% from 15:00Z to 16:54Z with no self-recovery; rollback does not relieve it
All writes to the shared ledger-db fail with 'No space left on device' — payment-service (354 errors), order-service (236 errors), and settlement-service all degraded at the same ~15:00Z onset
payment-service error rate jumps to ~61.5% at 15:00Z and stays ~60-64% through 16:55Z, persisting unchanged after the 15:12Z rollback

assumptions: The analytics_cdc slot is the dominant (not necessarily sole) consumer of the freed-retention headroom; the smooth 13.5-point ramp is consistent with slot-mediated WAL growth but quantified WAL/slot retention size was never directly retrieved
The trigger/activation of the slot retaining WAL at ~13:02Z is not recorded as a change event and is presumed chronic/unmonitored infra behaviour
portfolio-service (the fourth shared writer) is effectively immune because it is read-mostly / low-write / touches different tables — not because the shared-disk fault is payment-specific

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared ledger-db walking a chronic disk-usage ceiling under aggregate multi-writer load (capacity saturation)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The shared ledger-db's disk was on a chronic trajectory toward its capacity limit under aggregate multi-writer load (order, portfolio, payment, settlement), with WAL retention (analytics_cdc) as the dominant but not sole consumer of headroom; the failure is capacity saturation of the shared datastore. Origin is the shared datastore's capacity, and the v6.0.0 release is coincidental. This shares the SAME origin (ledger-db disk reaching capacity) as H2 and differs only in the accounting of which consumer(s) filled the disk; it is a secondary-detail variant of H2, retained separately only to record that the exact apportionment of the fill (slot-only vs aggregate) is unmeasured.

causal_chain.claim: Ledger-db disk climbs steadily under multi-writer load from four services (order, portfolio, payment, settlement)
Disk crosses its capacity ceiling at ~15:00Z with a smooth 86->100% ramp that began hours earlier and is unaffected by the 14:46Z deploy
Hard write failures begin across the co-tenant writers at the same onset
payment-service error rate spikes ~15:00Z and persists post-rollback

assumptions: Disk growth is not solely attributable to the analytics_cdc slot but includes aggregate write/retention pressure from the four co-tenants
The exact apportionment between slot-retained WAL and base-table growth was never measured

ranked_hypotheses.statement: A change to ledger-db's schema/retention or to a shared messaging/schema component in the same window is the true fault, causing the disk to fill; the fault origin would be the shared component, not payment-service code.

facts.statement: Every payment-service ERROR log since 14:00Z (354 of them) is the single pattern 'ledger write failed: ERROR: could not extend file: No space left on device', first at 15:00:26Z — a disk-full DB error, not a validation/constraint error or timeout.

ledger-db's own logs show disk usage escalating from 13:10:01Z ('disk usage 90%'), 95% at 14:15:45Z and 98% at 14:48:20Z, with WAL retained by an inactive replication slot ('analytics_cdc', tens of GB at a time) repeatedly from 13:02Z.

ledger-db emitted hard disk-full errors from 15:01:01Z: 'PANIC: could not write to file "pg_wal/xlogtemp.37478": No space left on device' (153 occurrences) and 'could not extend file "base/16402/2619"' (139 occurrences) from 15:01:39Z — DB-level failure onset ~1 minute after the payment-service error spike.

ledger-db disk_used_pct followed a smooth monotonic ramp: 86.57% (12:30Z) -> 89.37% (13:00Z) -> 90.40% (13:12Z) -> 94.76% (14:00Z) -> 97.48% (14:30Z) -> 98.52% (14:42Z) -> 99.88% (14:54Z), with no step change at the 14:46Z deploy.

disk_used_pct was already above 86% at the start of the window (12:30Z) and crossed 90% by 13:12Z — ~1h34m before the 14:46Z v6.0.0 deploy — so the ~13.5 points of headroom were consumed before, not after, the release.
disk_used_pct was pinned at exactly 100% from the 15:00Z bucket all the way to 16:54Z (every 6-min bucket avg 100.0), with no self-recovery for >2 hours.
payment-service error_rate jumped from a ~0.18-0.28% baseline to 61.52% in the 15:00:00Z 5-minute bucket and stayed ~60-64% through 16:55Z (last clean bucket 14:55:00Z at avg 0.18).

Post-rollback persistence is confirmed on complete, reliable metrics: error_rate stayed elevated (~55-70%; mean 62.29) in every 5-min bucket from 15:10Z through 16:55Z (still 61.10 at 16:55Z) with missing_points 0 and partial=false over 110 points — the 15:12Z rollback produced no visible drop.
settlement-service error_rate was flat ~0.17-0.23% through the 14:45Z bucket, jumped to avg 18.07% at the 14:54Z bucket and sustained ~54-56% through 16:51Z — mirroring payment-service's onset.
order-service error_rate was flat ~0.20-0.23% through the 14:45Z bucket, jumped to avg 16.17% at the 14:54Z bucket and sustained ~47-49% through 16:51Z.

order-service's writes are failing with the SAME disk-full signature as payment-service: 236 ERROR logs, all the single pattern 'INSERT INTO orders failed: No space left on device orderId=<n>', spanning 15:00:42Z-16:57:47Z.

portfolio-service (the fourth shared-ledger-db writer) did NOT degrade: error_rate stayed at baseline ~0.15-0.23% across the whole 15:00Z-16:51Z window (mean 0.21, max 0.32), with only 1 benign WARN log, zero ERROR logs, and db_pool_in_use flat ~11.9-12.0 connections.

The only deployment across all services between 12:00Z and 16:59Z is payment-service v6.0.0 (dep-6203) at 14:46:00Z ('New UPI mandate flow'; changes 'mandate create/approve endpoints' and 'new ledger entry type MANDATE_HOLD'), already status 'rolled_back' at 15:12:00Z.

There were zero config/flag changes across all services in the 12:00Z-16:59Z window and zero scoped to ledger-db in a widened 12:00Z-17:30Z window; separately, zero config/flag changes across all services in 15:00Z-17:00Z and zero scoped to ledger-db over 15:00Z-17:30Z.
No deployment of any kind occurred between 15:00Z and 17:00Z across all services (count 0), and no ledger-db deployment is recorded in 15:00Z-17:30Z (count 0).

ledger-db is a SHARED postgres datastore (shared:true, owner 'platform') written by four services — order-service, portfolio-service, payment-service and settlement-service — so a shared-infra fault is expected to affect more than payment-service.

There is no 'ledger-service' in the environment (get_service_dependencies returned not_found; known_services lists only ledger-db, user-db, redis-cache, kafka as shared infra), so all ledger writes go to the shared ledger-db via its calling services; ledger-db has its own telemetry and emits its own disk/PANIC logs.

Prior ledger-write-failure incidents resolved via infrastructure/DB fixes, not application rollback: HIST-114 (2025-04-18, ledger-db 'disk full from retained WAL', symptoms 'no space left on device'/'write failures', fixed by 'Dropped slot; added slot-lag alert') is the closest precedent; HIST-110 was fixed by provisioned IOPS; payment-failure precedent HIST-105 was an external bank-partner outage.
No current-incident (2026-06-01) record mentions an analytics_cdc slot drop or any WAL/slot cleanup; HIST-114 is a 2025 precedent mechanism, not a record of a 2026-06-01 cleanup.
payment-service p99 latency shows no degradation (flat ~292-348 ms across 14:00Z-16:55Z; 322.49 ms at 15:00Z, 315.98 ms at 16:55Z) — consistent with a hard write error rather than latency/saturation.

recommended_actions.action: IMMEDIATE MITIGATION: Free disk on the shared ledger-db — terminate/drop the inactive retaining replication slot 'analytics_cdc' (pg_drop_replication_slot) and force WAL checkpoint/retention release, then confirm disk_used_pct falls from 100%. This is the fix that resolved the matching precedent HIST-114 ('Dropped slot; added slot-lag alert').
recommended_actions.rationale: Disk exhaustion on shared ledger-db is the root cause; the retaining inactive slot is the dominant fill driver. Dropping the slot is the proven remediation from the closest precedent, not a rollback.

recommended_actions.action: IMMEDIATE: Confirm recovery by watching payment-service, order-service and settlement-service error_rate return toward baseline (~0.2%) and ledger-db disk_used_pct drop below 100% after the slot/WAL cleanup; roll back any remaining non-essential writer load if disk does not free promptly.
recommended_actions.rationale: Verifies the mitigation actually restores write capacity; error_rate recovery is the operational success signal and distinguishes cleanup-driven recovery from continued saturation.

recommended_actions.action: IMMEDIATE (do not repeat): Do NOT treat the v6.0.0 rollback as the fix — it has already been applied at 15:12Z and error_rate remained ~60% through 16:55Z; keep the rollback only if independently justified, not as the remedy for this incident.
recommended_actions.rationale: Post-rollback persistence on complete metrics falsifies the deployment as the cause, so relying on rollback will not restore service.

recommended_actions.action: SHORT TERM: Add a slot-lag / replication-slot retention alert and a ledger-db disk-headroom alert (warn at ~80%, page at ~90%) so a retaining inactive slot is caught before disk reaches 100%.
recommended_actions.rationale: The disk ramp ran 86%->100% over ~2.5h with only log thresholds and no alerting; the HIST-114 fix explicitly added a slot-lag alert, and this recurrence shows it was missing or ineffective.

recommended_actions.action: SHORT TERM: Audit and clean up inactive/orphaned replication slots on the shared ledger-db and configure a retention cap (e.g. max_slot_wal_keep_size) so a single inactive slot cannot retain WAL to disk-full.
recommended_actions.rationale: Root mechanism is a single inactive slot retaining tens of GB of WAL; capping retention bounds the blast radius across all four co-tenant writers.

recommended_actions.action: SHORT TERM: Repair / drain the analytics_cdc consumer (or formally decommission it) and verify its slot is either active-and-lagging-within-bounds or removed, with a follow-up review of why it retained WAL from ~13:02Z with no recorded trigger.
recommended_actions.rationale: The slot 'analytics_cdc' is inactive and its activation at ~13:02Z has no recorded change event; without addressing the consumer, the slot will regrow.

recommended_actions.action: LONG TERM: Move the shared ledger-db to capacity/headroom planning that accounts for aggregate multi-writer load plus WAL retention (provisioned IOPS/storage auto-grow), explicitly noting that H2 and H5 name the same origin — the datastore reaching capacity. Track WAL retention and base-table growth apportionment with metrics.
recommended_actions.rationale: The residual uncertainty is apportionment between slot-retained WAL and aggregate base-table growth, but either way the shared datastore is the single point of failure for four services.

recommended_actions.action: LONG TERM: Make shared-infra faults distinguishable from app faults in runbooks: on a shared-DB disk-full signature ('No space left on device', xlogtemp PANIC), check co-tenant writers (order/settlement/portfolio) before considering application rollback.
recommended_actions.rationale: Three of four co-tenant writers broke together with the identical disk-full signature while the app-layer error pattern was a disk-full DB error, not a validation error; runbooks should route to infra remediation first.

data_gaps: No direct observation of the WAL/slot retention SIZE or an explicit WAL/slot telemetry series — the claim that analytics_cdc is the dominant filler rests on the ledger-db log observation of 'tens of GB' retained plus the smooth ramp, not on a quantified WAL byte count.

The exact apportionment of the disk fill between slot-retained WAL and aggregate base-table growth from the four co-tenants was never measured, which is the residual H2-vs-H5 distinction (same origin, different accounting).
The ~13:02Z activation of the retaining analytics_cdc slot has no recorded change event; zero config/deployment events were found for ledger-db or any service in the window.

No 2026-06-01 cleanup/slot-drop record exists: the deployment ledger shows no ledger-db deployment or config change 15:00Z-17:30Z, and incident records contain no current-incident cleanup entry — so the recovery mechanism is inferred from the HIST-114 precedent, not observed.
The incident was still active at the latest data (16:54Z/16:55Z); no confirmation of recovery (error_rate back to ~0.2%, disk <100%) is available within the window.
portfolio-service's immunity is unexplained at the data level (no finer-grained pool/latency or write-path check), bounding how universally the shared-infra blast radius can be claimed.
settlement-service ERROR/WARN log query returned total_matched=0, so its ~55% error_rate could not be confirmed at the log level to be the same disk-full DB signature (order-service's was, F33).
order-service ERROR log result was truncated (236 matched, 15 returned), so a minority of non-disk-full error signatures in the unreturned records cannot be fully excluded.

what_would_change_the_conclusion: Evidence that ledger-db disk_used_pct did NOT ramp before 14:46Z (e.g. a step change coincident with the deploy) — would revive H1/H6 as release-triggered. Current data directly contradicts this (F21, F22).

Evidence that only payment-service degraded while order-service and settlement-service (which never ran v6.0.0) stayed healthy — would point to a payment-specific origin. Current data contradicts this (F31, F32, F33, F36).
Evidence that payment-service error_rate recovered promptly after the 15:12Z rollback — would support a deployment cause. Current data contradicts this (F19, F20).
A verified (non-disk-full) schema/validation rejection of the MANDATE_HOLD entry type in payment-service logs — would revive H1. The observed error signature is exclusively disk-full (F2).

Discovery that the error signature is actually an upstream/external failure (bank-partner-api/KYC) or a latency saturation, with flat disk usage — would revive H4. Flat p99 latency and DB-layer PANICs contradict this (F5, F4).

Direct evidence that a different consumer (aggregate base-table growth, not the analytics_cdc slot) filled the disk — would shift the origin-accounting toward H5 (though the origin, ledger-db capacity, and the fix remain the same).
Evidence that a ledger-db config/deployment change did occur in the window (contradicting the zero-count change queries) — would revive H3.
